articles.title: The Dunning-Kruger Effect, Now Available at Enterprise Scale
articles.summary: The Dunning-Kruger Effect, Now Available at Enterprise Scale The research is starting to coalesce, with different angles on whether AI is degrading human cognition or not. The right response is not panic--but it's also not dismissal. "Cognitive surrender" (outsourcing one's thinking to AI entirely for a given task) has been creeping into our current zeitgeist as a pre-accepted truth, and researchers have started to examine it more deeply. There are several papers that I think deserve serious attention from anyone making AI adoption decisions, and/or training their workforce in effective use of AI. In one, MIT Media Lab researchers strapped EEG headsets on 54 participants and measured brain activity while they wrote essays with ChatGPT, with a search engine, or with no tools at all. [1] In the second, MIT Sloan's Sinan Aral and Michael Caosun built a formal economic model showing how AI productivity gains rationally lead to skill erosion over time--what they call the "augmentation trap.

articles.title: I Ran My Business With AI for 30 Days: Results and Lessons
articles.summary: In February I handed my freelance business to an AI assistant. Not "used AI to help" — actually handed it over. Email responses, client communication, code reviews, architectural decisions, invoicing. I gave it access to everything and set one rule: do not ask me for approval unless a decision would cost more than €500. The reasoning was at least semi-serious. I'd been reading too many posts about AI productivity gains, and I wanted to measure what a developer with my experience actually offloads versus what requires real judgment. I expected to learn something useful. I did. Just not what I expected. This is a weekly account of what happened. Week 1: Suspiciously Good The first thing I noticed: my email response time improved from "usually same day" to "typically within 4 minutes." Clients noticed. articles.title: AI keeps getting blamed for tech layoffs, but the numbers don't really line up
articles.summary: I keep seeing "AI took these jobs" every time a company does layoffs, and I'm not convinced it's the main driver. A few things I keep coming back to. The industry cut around 122,500 jobs in 2025, down from about 153,000 in 2024. AI was named as a direct reason in fewer than 8% of those announcements. So for the other 90 percent plus, something else was going on. Actual AI adoption inside companies is also lower than the marketing suggests. Full org-wide rollout is still in the single digits in the surveys I've seen. Plenty of teams have a ChatGPT subscription and call themselves "AI-driven", but that is not the same as AI doing real work in the pipeline. My read: AI usually isn't replacing people directly. Managers see devs shipping more code and assume they can cut headcount, and companies are moving tight budgets toward expensive AI infra and tooling. articles.title: Most Companies Don't Have an AI Problem. They Have a Decision-Making Problem.
articles.summary: Most companies don't have an AI problem—they have a decision-making problem. AI amplifies existing organizational behaviors; it doesn't fix broken processes. Companies with unclear ownership, conflicting metrics, and slow decision-making often struggle to realize value from AI investments. The biggest barriers to AI adoption are frequently operational, not technical. Successful AI initiatives typically start with a single workflow, a measurable outcome, and clear accountability. Data quality matters, but alignment on priorities and decision rights often matters more. As AI increases employee leverage, decision quality becomes an even greater competitive advantage. Organizations that combine operational discipline with AI capabilities will outperform those that focus solely on technology. The winners in the AI era won't necessarily have the best models—they'll have the clearest and fastest decision-making systems.Read All
